title: Entanglement asymmetry and quantum Mpemba effect for Kramers-Wannier duality
authors: Milo Vescovo, Pasquale Calabrese, Filiberto Ares
abstract: The Kramers-Wannier duality is the prototypical example of a non-invertible symmetry, yet little is known about its fate away from criticality and out of equilibrium. We introduce the Kramers-Wannier entanglement asymmetry, a quantum-information measure that quantifies the breaking of this non-invertible symmetry in the transverse-field Ising chain. We first investigate its equilibrium properties, showing that it exhibits a striking crossover between the ordered and disordered phases together with a pronounced dip at the critical point that becomes increasingly sharp with subsystem size. We then study quantum quenches from both gapped phases to criticality and show that the Kramers-Wannier entanglement asymmetry decays to zero, signaling the dynamical restoration of the non-invertible symmetry. Remarkably, we uncover the emergence of a quantum Mpemba effect: under suitable conditions, states initially farther from equilibrium restore the Kramers-Wannier symmetry faster than states prepared closer to it. We provide both analytical and numerical evidence for this phenomenon and identify the mechanism responsible for its occurrence. Our work establishes entanglement asymmetry as a powerful probe of non-invertible symmetries beyond equilibrium and opens new perspectives on the dynamics of dualities in quantum many-body systems.
summary: This theoretical paper introduces the Kramers-Wannier entanglement asymmetry as a measure to probe non-invertible symmetries in quantum many-body systems like the Ising chain. Key findings include demonstrating that this asymmetry decays dynamically during quenches, revealing a novel quantum Mpemba effect where far-from-equilibrium states relax faster than near-equilibrium ones.
main_problem: The study investigates the fate of the Kramers-Wannier duality, a non-invertible symmetry, when moving away from critical points and into non-equilibrium dynamics.
main_result: The authors demonstrate the emergence of a quantum Mpemba effect, where states initially farther from equilibrium restore the broken symmetry faster than those prepared closer to it. They also characterize the asymptotic decay of entanglement asymmetry during quenches.
method: The analysis employs quantum information measures, specifically the Kramers-Wannier entanglement asymmetry ($\Delta S$), calculated using techniques involving dual reduced density matrices and replica tricks for fermionic systems.
model_or_system: The primary model is the transverse-field Ising chain, analyzed through its mapping to a quadratic fermionic Hamiltonian. The study examines both equilibrium ground states and non-equilibrium dynamics following quantum quenches.
key_observables: Kramers-Wannier entanglement asymmetry ($\Delta S$), which quantifies the breaking of the non-invertible symmetry; the asymptotic decay rate $\sim t^{-3}$.
important_parameters: The transverse field $h$, with criticality occurring at $h=1$; subsystem size $\ell$; and time evolution parameters characterizing the initial quench state ($h_0$).
main_assumptions: The derivation of asymptotic decay relies on conjectures regarding the Widom-Szegő formula, and the procedure for defining the dual reduced density matrix ($\hat{ho}_A$) is adopted as an alternative to direct duality application.
figures_summary: Not specified by notes; however, results show crossovers in equilibrium asymmetry and a time decay profile demonstrating the Mpemba effect during quenches.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the KW entanglement asymmetry for non-invertible symmetries (equilibrium analysis) to studying its behavior after quantum quenches. The core development involves deriving the long-time asymptotics of this asymmetry, leading to the identification and characterization of the Mpemba effect.
why_interesting: The work provides a powerful new diagnostic tool ($\Delta S$) for probing non-invertible symmetries in many-body systems beyond equilibrium, which is highly relevant for understanding thermalization and dynamics in quantum materials.
